title: EscrowFinish fulfillment fees: XRP drops and SGD prices in the app
abstract: Measured Testnet costs and accounting: how XRP drops differ from the SGD price shown in the app, including principal and fees.
tags: EscrowFinish fulfillment fees and XRP drops
body:
EscrowFinish with a fulfillment has a higher fee than a plain XRP Payment. Our observed Testnet conditional finish used 423 drops. EscrowCreate used 12 drops, so the measured purchase overhead was 435 drops before a separate answer anchor. These are historical observations rather than a promise about future network load. A price displayed in SGD is an application accounting unit; it is not the network fee and it is not a market exchange rate.

This is a team-authored adaptation of docs/key-reveal-escrow.md, read alongside docs/key-reveal-escrow.md and docs/x402-xrpl.md. The evidence describes our Testnet implementation and dated observations. It does not establish production readiness, independent writer participation or financial adoption. The authors are the ResearchAgent builders; their involvement must remain visible wherever the article is purchased or cited.

The implementation record explains the boundary this way: Conditional finish costs more than a Payment. The XRPL fee formula scales as base_fee × (33 + fulfillment_bytes / 16) before multisign/load effects. Here K is 32 bytes and its encoded fulfillment is 36 bytes. At the observed 12-drop signing base, ceil(12 × (33 + 36/16)) = 423 drops. A 2,000-drop cap rejects excessive fees. Live create/cancel each cost 12 drops. A cancelled 60,000-drop principal is fully returned; its buyer still pays 24 drops in fees. - Synthetic corpus and extractive fixture answers in the proof are labelled; Testnet value transfer is real Testnet execution, with no real value. For a reader assessing this result, the operative distinction is between a documented mechanism and a freshly verified transaction. Reproduction requires checking the actual receipt and its ledger evidence, rather than treating this note as a live network probe.

The implementation record explains the boundary this way: Live purchase activity and receipts show validated create and finish links, the publication ledger, and separate policy results for key/Condition binding and ciphertext authentication/decryption. A pending CancelAfter countdown is advisory; only a validated EscrowCancel reports principal returned. Historical receipts without the new check fields do not acquire check marks by inference. For a reader assessing this result, the operative distinction is between a documented mechanism and a freshly verified transaction. Reproduction requires checking the actual receipt and its ledger evidence, rather than treating this note as a live network probe.

The implementation record explains the boundary this way: UC3's failed signed passage promise can be challenged after EscrowFinish. Policy reopens the authenticated envelope privately; no failed plaintext enters a grant, snapshot or model. The publisher validates its persisted finish before recording the settlement for the existing write-once refund journal. The refund is a separate Payment whose InvoiceID is the finish hash. Replacement expertise uses a new intent and escrow; gross budget authorization is not replenished by the refund. Multi-origin key-reveal intent identifiers hash the complete source identity, run and round to fit the existing 200-character quote limit. For a reader assessing this result, the operative distinction is between a documented mechanism and a freshly verified transaction. Reproduction requires checking the actual receipt and its ledger evidence, rather than treating this note as a live network probe.

The implementation record explains the boundary this way: An envelope that cannot authenticate/decrypt, or lacks a failed passage claim, cannot support the passage challenge and remains quarantined and charged. Unsupported escrow writers remain skipped with no exact-payment fallback. Caller hire funding, royalties, change and refunds remain explicit Payments; they are transfers rather than purchases of encrypted article delivery. Simulated make run remains unchanged. No gates or test thresholds were loosened. For a reader assessing this result, the operative distinction is between a documented mechanism and a freshly verified transaction. Reproduction requires checking the actual receipt and its ledger evidence, rather than treating this note as a live network probe.

A refund after successful key publication is a separate writer-signed Payment. The ledger does not decide whether prose is useful, truthful or worth its price. A signed passage promise and a verifiable fraud proof establish responsibility for a broken commitment, but a real writer could refuse a refund. The fixture writer cooperates in our demonstrations. This limitation belongs beside the transaction evidence so that a reader does not mistake a cooperative recovery for unilateral buyer protection.
